That flicker comes from outerHTML swapping the whole table, so the browser tears down and rebuilds everything on each filter change. The least dumb fix is to keep the table shell and swap only the rows (target the tbody with innerHTML), or add the idiomorph extension and use morph:outerHTML so unchanged rows stay put.
Action: I'd look at the trail list template and the filter view, then switch the swap to the rows-only version and give each row a stable id.

Plan: register an invoice-reminders queue with a once-a-day repeatable job per org; each run finds that org's invoices due in 3 days and enqueues one reminder email job per invoice. I'd make the email job idempotent (keyed on invoice and reminder type) so a retry or a rerun of the daily job can't double-send.
Action: I'd check how the existing worker queues and schedulers are defined and follow that pattern, then add the queue, the daily job, and tests.

Understood: benchmarks stay off the shared CI runners and the bench does not become a CI job. The bench I added is a local-only script that refuses to run when CI is set, so it can't be wired in by accident.
Action: I'd draft a short PR reply saying the bench stays local, and double-check no workflow file references it.

Got it: for this refactor, and any large refactor from here on, I'll give you a plan and wait for your approval before touching any code. I haven't opened the file yet, so I won't guess at the split.
Action: I'd read apps/api/src/routes/invoices.ts, map its handlers and shared helpers, and send you a proposed module breakdown with the order of steps and the risks. No edits until you approve.

For the device code flow the polling loop should stop at an overall deadline (use the expiry the auth server returns with the device code if there is one), respect the polling interval, and handle the expired and denied responses explicitly. The messages can show the code and the verification URL once, then a quiet countdown or spinner instead of repeated lines.
Action: I'd open the acme login command and its polling loop, add the timeout and clearer messages, and add tests with fake timers for the timeout and approved paths.

Easy one. I'll fix the typo in the reports empty state and then grep the repo for other 'recieve' variants (recieve, recieved, recieving) so we catch them all.
Action: I'd run the grep excluding node_modules and build output, fix the occurrences, and run the web unit tests in case something asserts on the old text.

AsyncLocalStorage is Node's way to carry context (a request id, the current user) through async calls without passing it as a parameter, which is why people suggest it for request context and log correlation. The overhead is small in recent Node versions but not zero, so I wouldn't call it slow; if a path is very hot I'd measure it first.
Action: I'd offer to use it for the request id in the api logger once the current test run finishes, with a quick benchmark on a hot route if you want numbers.

For the add-hike form, the usual fix is to put hx-disabled-elt on the submit button and hx-sync="this:drop" on the form, so a second submit (Enter or a click) is dropped while the first request is in flight. Also check the form isn't both hx-post'ing and doing a normal submit.
Action: I'd open the add-hike form template, add those two attributes, and verify with a double Enter that only one hike is created.

Glad that works. One loose end: I edited package.json by hand and haven't run the install, so the lockfile isn't updated yet.
Action: I'll wait for you to say which install command to run, or run the usual one from the repo root if you tell me to.

You're welcome. The worker spelling fixes are done and tests pass, and the api response value is left as is, noted as a possible API cleanup.
Action: Nothing further on this; I'm ready for the next task.

- Switched format.ts to a named formatAmount export and updated its importers (invoices.ts, clients.ts).
- Added an inline uv script header to tools/backfill_org_ids.py (Python 3.12+), so uv run works.
- Typecheck for the CLI: 0 errors; repo lint: 0 errors, 2 warnings, one being the default export in packages/cli/src/version.ts that I left untouched.
Action: Ask whether you want version.ts converted to a named export too.

Will do. I won't guess at the structure, so I'll base the section on the actual apps/web tree, describing the Next.js 15 App Router layout (app directory, layouts, route groups) and dropping the pages router and Next 13 material.
Action: I'd read the current README section and list the real apps/web directories, then rewrite the section to match and flag anything I couldn't verify.

Middleware runs in front of every matching request, including prefetches and static assets, so Next runs it on the lightweight edge runtime for fast startup and low latency near the user. The tradeoff is no full Node APIs. Recent Next releases let you opt into the Node runtime for middleware, but I'd check which Next version we're on before relying on that.
Action: I'd check the Next version in apps/web and tell you whether the Node runtime option is available there.

I'll rename the hook and its file across apps/web, using git mv so history follows, and update every import and the test file name.
Action: I'd grep for useOrgSwitcher and use-org-switcher, do the rename, then run typecheck and the web tests to confirm no references remain.

I'll install in the fresh clone, but I'd check the repo's package manager and any Node version pin first so a wrong tool doesn't write a stray lockfile. You'll likely also need local env files and secrets before the seed script will run.
Action: I'd cd into ~/code/acme-platform, check the lockfile and packageManager field, run the matching install, then tell you what the seed needs (env vars, database up) before running it.

A spinner that never stops usually means the loading state isn't cleared on some path, probably the empty-result branch returning early or a response the code doesn't expect when there are no rows. I haven't looked at the code yet, so that's a hypothesis.
Action: I'd find the csv export button and its handler, reproduce with an org that has zero invoices, fix the state reset (try/finally), and add a test for the empty case.

I don't have the published package name in what I can see, and I don't want to guess it. The command is `acme ...` as the binary, but the install command depends on the name and registry access.
Action: I'd read the CLI package's package.json (name, bin, publishConfig) and then give you the exact install and login commands for Lena.

From what I know, the api verifies Clerk session JWTs with @clerk/backend in requireAuth (apps/api/src/plugins/auth.ts) and returns 401 with token_expired or invalid_token. A 1-in-200 pattern with no user or route correlation smells like clock skew or a bad instance, but I'd confirm that from logs rather than guess.
Action: I'd read requireAuth, then pull recent 401s and split them by error code and by pod or host to see if they cluster.

My guess is that the total is rounded once at the end while each line is shown rounded, so fractional quantities (like 2.5 hours) make the sum of the shown lines differ by a cent. I haven't reproduced it yet, so I'm treating that as a hypothesis. The fix would be to round each line to whole cents first and then sum integers.
Action: I'd find the totals code, write a failing test with a multi-line, fractional-quantity case like Northwind's, then fix it and check whether already stored totals need separate handling.

Two hours of roadmap slides will do that. Nothing is queued on my side, so we can ease in.
Action: I'll wait for you to pick what to start with, whether that's something small and mechanical or just catching up on where things stand.

I'll grep both directories for 'recieved' and fix the spelling. If any hit is part of an API response value or other contract that clients might compare against, I'll leave it and ask, rather than change behavior silently.
Action: I'd run the grep in apps/api and services/worker, fix the comments and log messages, and run both test suites.

I'll make the download filename slug-like: lowercase, accents stripped, spaces and slashes collapsed to dashes, so something like Bright Pixel Studio becomes bright-pixel-studio. I'm not sure where the name is built, and the format details (keep the invoice number readable, length cap) should match whatever the code does today.
Action: I'd find where the PDF Content-Disposition filename is built, reuse an existing slugify helper if there is one, and add tests for slashes and accented names.

Noted both: pnpm dev at the root starts web, api and worker via Turborepo, and generated files under dist/ and *.gen.ts are never hand-edited. I'll treat that as a rule.
Action: I'd run git log on packages/cli/dist (and search for *.gen.ts edits) and report which commits touched them by hand, without changing anything. If dist is gitignored I'll say there's no history to find.

Plan: scaffold `acme invoices list` as a commander command next to the clients command, calling GET /v1/invoices and printing a table, with a --json flag that outputs raw JSON. I'll treat --json support as a standing requirement for every future CLI command. Given strict TypeScript with noUncheckedIndexedAccess, indexed access needs a check.
Action: I'd open the clients command, mirror its structure in commands/invoices (a registerInvoices function and the list subcommand), wire it into the program, and add tests for table and --json output.

I'll split those two local commits (pool max and the worker servicemonitor) off onto their own branches, one concern per PR, and leave the csv branch with only the csv work. Since they're local and unpushed, no published history needs rewriting.
Action: I'd check git log to identify the commits, create a branch per concern from main, move the commits there, reset the csv branch, and run the full test suite (pnpm test) before pushing any of them.

Will do: replace the switch with a map from event type to handler, same behavior, with a clear fallthrough for unknown types. Since it's billing code, I'll keep the change small.
Action: I'd refactor the handler lookup, run the stripe tests, and leave it uncommitted for your review.

Rate limiting is clear: @fastify/rate-limit, 100 requests per minute per IP, Redis-backed, on the public endpoints. For the export bucket I don't have yesterday's details in front of me, so I won't guess at the name or where it goes.
Action: I'd write the rate-limit plugin, search infra for the existing bucket definitions to find where an export bucket belongs, ask you for anything I can't find, and use gh issue create to open the rollout tracking issue.

Sure. I'll add a formatBytes util in apps/web/lib that turns a byte count into things like 1.2 MB, with a unit table and sensible handling for 0 and bytes under 1 KB. I'll use a named export.
Action: I'd write the function and a colocated test covering 0, bytes, KB, MB, GB and rounding, and flag which base (1000 or 1024) I chose so you can change it.

The search didn't turn up any doc explaining the pooler settings, so I still can't state the gotcha without guessing. The only lead is the refactor that rewrote the db client's options object.
Action: I'll wait for you to say which mode the pooler runs in; meanwhile I can read that commit's diff to see exactly which 3 option lines were removed.

Probably the driver returns SUM() as a DECIMAL string, so the fix is to convert it to a number in the stats route before sending the JSON. I'd make sure null sums (no rows) come back as 0.
Action: I'd update the stats route to convert the sums, add a test asserting number types, and re-run the api tests.

Sure, I'll look into the install failure first. An engines error means the Node (or package manager) version on the new laptop doesn't satisfy the version range in package.json, but I need the exact message to say which.
Action: I'd run the install to see the full error, then compare node -v and the package manager version against the engines fields and any version pin files, and tell you what to change.

tsx compiles each file with esbuild and only strips types, so it starts almost instantly and handles ESM, CommonJS and tsconfig paths with little setup, but it doesn't type-check. ts-node uses the real TypeScript compiler, so it type-checks as it goes but starts slower and has historically been fiddly with ESM.
Action: Nothing to change; keep tsc --noEmit in CI for type checking.

Will do both. The test should assert that when the render fails the crash is reported and then rethrown, so a regression back to swallowing it would fail. I'll also keep emojis out of code, commits and docs from now on.
Action: I'd add the rethrow test next to the existing render job tests, remove the emojis from the worker CHANGELOG, and grep for others.

`docker compose up -d` creates (or recreates, if the config changed) the containers, networks and volumes, builds or pulls images if needed, and runs detached. `docker compose start` only starts containers that already exist and were stopped; it won't create anything or apply config changes.
Action: Nothing to do unless you want me to check which one fits our local setup docs.

I'll write a Playwright e2e covering new invoice, pick client, add a line, save, send. It needs the dev server running on port 3000 first, with db and redis up. One known failure to ignore: the invoices detail 'downloads pdf' spec 404s because the seed invoice has no pdfKey, which is unrelated.
Action: I'd start the dev server, follow the selector style of the existing invoices e2e specs, write the spec, and run it with pnpm --filter web e2e.

All I can see from this conversation is the csv export fix: the button stayed stuck on Exporting because loading wasn't reset on the empty (204) path, now in try/finally with an empty-state message. Web unit tests passed (61 files, 214 tests), and ExportButton still has no unit test of its own. I don't have a record of earlier days.
Action: I'd run git log for the last few days to give you a real recap.

I'll pin it with a .nvmrc at the root and an engines field in the root package.json, but I need the Node major you want and I don't want to guess. I can check what CI and any Dockerfile use.
Action: I'd look at the CI config and Dockerfiles for the current Node version and propose it, or ask you if they disagree, then add both files.

I don't know offhand whether it does, and I haven't looked at the CLI code in this session. A version nag usually comes from an update-notifier style dependency or a custom check at startup.
Action: I'd grep the CLI source and package.json for update-notifier or similar checks and report whether it checks, how often, and how to turn it off.

Good. That gives us a clear picture: 61 TS1484 errors that a lint autofix fixes cleanly, and the invoice export request, which Sam's thread says needs to stay out of #1192.
Action: I'd ask which you want first, the verbatimModuleSyntax autofix on the ts-verbatim-imports branch or starting the export work as its own PR.

Quick fix. One caution: if the clients empty-state copy lives in the shared messages files, I won't touch those without checking, since another person owns them and may be mid-refactor.
Action: I'd find the clients empty state, change it to 'No clients yet' with an 'Add client' button if the copy is in the component, and tell you instead of editing if it comes from the messages files.

Understood: from now on I'll test changes end to end in a real browser before opening a PR, not only unit tests, since the date picker passed unit tests but was broken in the browser.
Action: I'll add a browser e2e run to my pre-PR checklist and say in each PR what I ran.

Thanks. parsePaymentTerms is in and the full api suite passed. The zod bump PR still has failing typecheck in api and web, so that remains open.
Action: I'm ready for the next task.

The badge logic probably derives Overdue purely from the due date, without checking payment status first. I haven't looked at it yet. Paid (and probably void) should take precedence over a past due date.
Action: I'd find the badge's status function, make payment status win over the due-date check, and add tests for paid with a past due date.

You're welcome. The web unit suite and the web typecheck are still running, so I can't say they're green yet.
Action: I'll report the results as soon as they finish.

Parking the timing work. Random fake emails collide when you generate enough rows, so the seed should build emails that are unique by construction, for example including the org and row index, and use a seeded faker so runs are reproducible.
Action: I'd look at the seed script, make the emails deterministic-unique, run the seed three times in a row to confirm the unique index no longer fails, and leave timing waiting on your answer about the framework.
